segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now about the things of the Spirit, brothers and sisters, I do not want you to be uninformed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You know that when you were Gentiles, you were carried off to idols that cannot speak, however you happened to be led.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I am making known to you that no one speaking by the Spirit of God says,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Jesus is accursed,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and no one can say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Jesus is Lord,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: except by the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There are different allotments of gifts, but the same Spirit;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and there are different allotments of service, and the same Lord;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and there are different allotments of workings, but the same God, who works all of them in everyone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For to one a message of wisdom is given through the Spirit, to another a message of knowledge according to the same Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to another workings of deeds of power, to another prophecy, to another the distinguishing of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But one and the same Spirit works all these, allotting to each one individually just as he wills.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For just as the body is one and has many parts, and all the parts of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free—and we were all given one Spirit to drink.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For indeed the body is not one part but many.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If the foot should say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: it does not for that reason stop belonging to the body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if the ear should say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: it does not for that reason stop belonging to the body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as it is, God has placed the parts, each one of them, in the body just as he wanted.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If they were all one part, where would the body be?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as it is, there are many parts, yet one body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The eye cannot say to the hand,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I have no need of you,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: nor again the head to the feet,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I have no need of you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are all the more necessary,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the parts of the body we think less honorable we clothe with greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are made all the more presentable,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: while our presentable parts have no such need. But God has composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacks it,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that there may be no division in the body, but the parts may have the same concern for one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if one part suffers, all the parts suffer with it; if one part is honored, all the parts rejoice with it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now you are the body of Christ, and individually parts of it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And God has placed in the assembly first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then deeds of power, then gifts of healing, acts of help, acts of guidance, kinds of tongues.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work deeds of power?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But be eager for the greater gifts. And further, I will show you a way beyond all comparison.

notes.note: The Greek is a bare adjective, “the spiritual,” with no noun. Most translations supply “gifts,” but the word for “gift” first appears in verse 4, so the broader phrase is used here. The form could also be masculine, “spiritual people,” meaning those who claimed special endowment by the Spirit; a minority of interpreters read it that way.

The Greek word means “nations” and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples; it is the same word translated “nations” elsewhere. Paul speaks as though his largely non-Jewish readers are no longer Gentiles, which is why many modern translations say “pagans” here.

In the Greek Old Testament this word names something handed over to God for destruction, and so something under a curse. Why anyone would say this of Jesus is disputed: it may reflect rejection of a crucified Messiah, utterances in pagan worship, or simply a hypothetical opposite to the confession “Jesus is Lord.”

The noun can mean either “difference, variety” or “distribution, apportionment.” The related verb in verse 11 plainly means “distribute,” and this rendering keeps that link visible. Most translations prefer “varieties,” which is also lexically sound, and the contrast with “the same Spirit” implies variety on either reading.

The Greek word was an everyday term for service or for a task carried out on someone's behalf, not a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests clergy or a profession. Several modern translations also use “service” in this verse.

The Greek is simply the plural of the ordinary word for “power,” used of concrete acts. “Miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering and the meaning is not in dispute. “Deeds of power” is used throughout this translation so that the connection with “power” stays visible.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for the tongue and for a language; a first-century reader would have heard “kinds of languages.” The traditional “tongues” is kept because it is the established name for this gift. Whether Paul means human languages unknown to the speaker or speech of another kind is debated.

The Greek word means a limb or organ of a body. “Member” once meant exactly that in English, but now mainly suggests belonging to a club or organization, which blurs the bodily image Paul develops through the rest of the chapter.

notes.traditional: by one Spirit; in one Spirit
notes.note: The Greek preposition can mark the Spirit as the element in which believers are baptized (“in”) or as the agent who baptizes (“by”). “In” is chosen because it matches the usual construction with “baptize” and fits the parallel image of drinking the Spirit. Many translations have “by.”

A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament's term for Israel assembled. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the one Greek word is always recognizable.

The word comes from the vocabulary of steering a ship. In the Greek Old Testament it is used for wise direction or counsel, as in Proverbs. Translations vary between “administration” and “leadership”; what activity Paul had in mind is not known in detail. Like the preceding term, it is plural in Greek and names activities, not offices.

The Greek form can be a command (“be eager for”) or a statement (“you are eager for”). Most translations take it as a command, in line with the clear command using the same verb in 14:1. A minority read it as a description, even a mild rebuke, of the Corinthians' ambition, which Paul then answers with the “way” of chapter 13.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs throughout the letters, and translators split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters,” and “friends.”
The word means both “tongue” and “language”; Acts 2, 1 Corinthians 12–14 and Revelation need one policy on “tongues” versus “languages.”
It recurs in Romans, 1 Corinthians, and the Pastorals, and it needs to be kept distinct from other “gift” words (δῶρον, δωρεά) and from πνευματικά.
The body-part image recurs in Romans 6 and 12, 1 Corinthians 6 and 12, Ephesians, Colossians and James, and “members” versus “parts” should not vary between chapters.
The substantive use (12:1; 14:1) and the adjective (2:13–15; 15:44–46; Romans; Ephesians) need a consistent policy on “spiritual” versus “of the Spirit” and on supplying “gifts.”
